summary: A landlocked mountainous country at the junction of Central and South Asia, long a crossroads of the Silk Road and a meeting place of many empires. Its population is multiethnic, consisting mainly of Pashtuns, Tajiks, Hazaras and Uzbeks.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: In the mid-7th century Arab armies advanced eastward and Islam began to enter western Afghanistan; the Ghaznavid dynasty, which had Ghazni as its capital, and the later Ghurid dynasty of the 10th to 12th centuries were both Sunni regimes, making Sunni Islam the common faith of Pashtuns, Tajiks and Uzbeks. The Hanafi school predominates, and after the Durrani Empire was founded in 1747 it also drew its legitimacy to rule from Sunni Islam, which is why about 85 percent of the population remains Sunni today.

ranking.name: Islam (Shia)
ranking.description: Shia Muslims are mainly the Hazaras of the central Hazarajat highlands. In the 16th century the Safavid dynasty promoted Shia Islam in Persia, and its influence reached neighboring Herat and the Hazara region. In the 1890s Emir Abdur Rahman Khan conquered the Hazarajat; large numbers of Hazaras were killed or enslaved, and they faced long-term discrimination afterward. They were also repeatedly persecuted under the Taliban (1996-2001 and again after 2021), so they have always remained a minority.

ranking.name: Others (Sikhism, Hinduism, etc.)
ranking.description: Sikhs and Hindus were mostly merchants who came from Punjab from the 19th century onward, running cloth and moneylending businesses in Kabul, Kandahar and Jalalabad. The civil wars from the 1980s and Taliban rule forced the great majority to flee to India, and after the 2018 Jalalabad bombing and the 2020 attack on a Sikh temple in Kabul almost all of them left; only a very small number remain today.

religion.background: Before the arrival of Islam, Afghanistan was a meeting ground of Zoroastrianism and Buddhism, as witnessed by the Gandharan Buddhist art of the Kushan Empire in the 2nd century and the Buddhas of Bamiyan carved around the 6th century. After the Arabs arrived from the 7th century, Islam replaced the older faiths around the 10th century; Sunni Islam was consolidated under the Ghaznavids, while Shia Islam took root among the Hazaras through the influence of Safavid Persia. After the Soviet invasion of 1979, religion became the rallying cry of the jihad against the Soviets; the Taliban established their regime in 1996 and destroyed the Buddhas of Bamiyan in 2001. Since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the situation of religious minorities has become even harder.

language.official: The official languages are Pashto and Dari (Afghan Persian).

ranking.name: Dari (Afghan Persian)
ranking.description: Dari is the Persian of Afghanistan. Since the Samanid dynasty of the 9th and 10th centuries, Persian has been the court and literary language of this region, and Herat became a center of Persian culture under the Timurid dynasty in the 15th century. Because it has long served as the language of administration, commerce and education, people of different ethnic groups communicate in it; the 1964 constitution formally called it 'Dari', and about half of the population speaks it as a mother tongue or first language of communication.

ranking.name: Pashto
ranking.description: Pashto is the mother tongue of the largest ethnic group, the Pashtuns. It belongs to the Eastern Iranian branch and is concentrated around Kandahar in the south and Jalalabad in the east, extending into northwestern Pakistan. After the Pashtun Ahmad Shah established the Durrani dynasty in 1747, the ruling class was mostly Pashtun; in 1936 the government declared Pashto a national language and promoted its teaching in schools, but because Persian has long been used in cities and in administration, its share of speakers is slightly lower than that of Dari.

ranking.name: Uzbek
ranking.description: Uzbek belongs to the Turkic language family and is spoken mainly in the northern provinces bordering Uzbekistan, such as Balkh, Jowzjan and Faryab. Some of these Uzbeks are descendants of settlers who arrived when the Shaybanid dynasty moved south in the 16th century, and others are refugees who fled Soviet collectivization in the 1920s and 1930s. The 2004 constitution recognizes it as a third official language in the areas where it is spoken.

ranking.name: Turkmen
ranking.description: Turkmen is also a Turkic language, and its speakers are concentrated in the northwest in places bordering Turkmenistan, such as Faryab and Jowzjan. Many Afghan Turkmen are descendants of families who moved south in the 1920s to escape Soviet suppression of the Basmachi movement and collectivization; they are famous for weaving Turkmen carpets, and the 2004 constitution lists their language alongside Uzbek as a regional official language.

language.history: In ancient Afghanistan, Eastern Iranian languages such as Bactrian were widely spoken; coins and inscriptions of the Kushan Empire wrote Bactrian in the Greek alphabet. After Islamization, New Persian became the court and literary language from the 9th and 10th centuries, and the 13th-century poet Rumi was born in the Balkh area. After the Durrani dynasty was founded in 1747 the status of Pashto rose, and in the 20th century the government promoted Pashto as a national language, but Dari remained the main language of the cities and of communication between ethnic groups. The 2004 constitution established Pashto and Dari as the official languages and recognized Uzbek, Turkmen and others as regional official languages.

ranking.name: Kabuli Palaw
ranking.description: Lamb or beef is stewed to make a broth, then steamed together with long-grain rice and topped with fried shredded carrots, raisins and almonds; the rice is flavored with meat juices and cumin.
ranking.history: Pilaf-type dishes originated in Persia and Central Asia and spread through this region over centuries with Silk Road trade. The name 'Kabuli' indicates that the dish took its form in upper-class households in the capital; in the past both rice and meat were expensive ingredients that only wealthy families could afford when entertaining guests. The raisins and almonds are dried fruits abundantly produced in Afghanistan. Today it is regarded as Afghanistan's national dish, and a large platter is always served at weddings, at Eid al-Fitr and when receiving guests.

ranking.name: Mantu
ranking.description: Thin dough wrappers are filled with onion and minced beef and steamed, then served topped with garlic yogurt sauce and a tomato and bean sauce and sprinkled with dried mint, so that tangy fragrance and meat juices blend together.
ranking.history: Like Turkish manti and Central Asian manti, mantu is generally thought to be a pasta dish that spread along the Silk Road with Turkic and Mongol peoples during the Mongol Empire in the 13th century, and its name may share an origin with the Chinese word 'mantou'. In Afghanistan it combines the Central Asian method of steamed dumplings with the yogurt sauce common in Persian and South Asian cooking, and it is a labor-intensive dish for festivals and hospitality. Afghan emigrants have also taken mantu to North America and Europe, where it has become a signature of Afghan restaurants abroad.

ranking.name: Bolani
ranking.description: Thin dough is filled with mashed potato, leek or pumpkin, folded into a half-moon and pan-fried until golden and crisp; it is usually cut into pieces and dipped in yogurt sauce.
ranking.history: Bolani is an everyday snack in Afghan households; the dough and leeks are inexpensive local ingredients, and vendors often fry them fresh in the markets. At sunset during Ramadan, when the fast is broken, households prepare a stack of bolani to eat with tea and yogurt. Potatoes only became widespread in Afghanistan after the 19th century, so the potato filling that is most common today is actually a later version, while the leek filling (gandana) is considered the more traditional flavor.

ranking.name: Ashak
ranking.description: Dumplings filled with leeks or scallions are boiled, laid over garlic yogurt, topped with tomato and meat sauce and sprinkled with dried mint, giving a light, tangy taste.
ranking.history: Like mantu, ashak belongs to the Central Asian dumpling family, but it has a vegetable filling, reflecting the leeks (gandana) commonly grown in Afghan courtyards. Because rolling out the dough and filling the dumplings is quite laborious, it is often a festive dish prepared together by female relatives and friends, and it is especially common at Eid al-Fitr and at Nowruz, the new year on 21 March. Nowruz is a spring equinox festival derived from the Persian Zoroastrian tradition, so ashak also carries a sense of welcoming spring.

ranking.name: Chapli Kebab
ranking.description: Minced beef or lamb is mixed with onion, tomato, coriander seeds and chili, pressed into large thin patties and fried in oil; they are spicy and juicy.
ranking.history: Chapli kebab originated in the Pashtun region, and its name is often explained as coming from the Pashto word 'chaprikh' (flat), since its shape is as broad and flat as a sandal sole. It is most famous at roadside stalls in eastern Afghanistan and around Peshawar in Pakistan, and it is a culinary tradition shared by Pashtuns on both sides of the Durand Line, drawn in 1893, which divides them between two countries. Today it is often eaten as a street lunch with naan, onion and yogurt.
